hook: The half-measures trap. Why "checking less often" keeps the problem exactly where it is.
topic: Why reduction without reset fails structurally
body:
**The half-measures trap. Checking less often doesn't fix the calibration — it maintains it.**

Here's the structural problem. Your dopamine threshold is set by the frequency and intensity of reward signals across your environment. Every time you check a feed — even if it's fewer times per day — you're resupplying the system at the level it's already calibrated to. You're maintaining the threshold, not lowering it.

Think of it as a water level. The threshold is the water line. Every high-stimulus check is a refill. Checking less often is a smaller refill. But if the level never drops far enough, the recalibration never triggers. The system stays set where it is.

This is why people who "use their phone less" often report no improvement in focus. They reduced the volume without dropping below the recalibration threshold. It feels like progress. The biology disagrees.

A real reset requires the stimulus level to drop below the current baseline and stay there long enough for the system to adjust downward. That requires a different class of intervention — not moderation. Architecture.

What that architecture looks like is in the link in bio.
